notes.h: Reproductive structures of a flowering plant
notes.b: Flowering plants reproduce sexually by means of flowers, which produce the gametes (sex cells) and bring about pollination (the transfer of pollen) and fertilisation (the joining of male and female gametes). Three structures carry the process from gamete to new plant: the flower, the seed and the fruit.
points: The flower is a short shoot whose parts are modified leaves arranged in rings (whorls) on the receptacle, the tip of the flower stalk. Its job is to produce gametes, bring about pollination and fertilisation, and then produce seeds and fruits.

The flower makes the male and female gametes and brings about pollination. It is the only one of the three structures that exists before fertilisation, because the seed and fruit develop from flower parts afterwards.

The seed, a fertilised and developed ovule, contains the embryo (a new plant) with a food store and a protective coat. The fruit, a developed ovary, protects the seeds and helps to disperse them, that is, spread them away from the parent plant.
Seed detail is in Seeds; dispersal is in Fruit and seed dispersal.
Many flowers are bisexual (hermaphrodite), meaning they have both male and female parts in the same flower, e.g. buttercup.

Some plants have separate male and female flowers on the same plant, e.g. hazel, whose male flowers hang in catkins and whose small female flowers have red stigmas. In some species male and female flowers are on different plants, e.g. holly.
notes.tip: Be ready to name the three reproductive structures and give the job of each: the flower makes gametes and brings about pollination, the seed holds the embryo, and the fruit protects the seeds and helps to disperse them.

notes.h: Flower structures: the outer parts and nectary
notes.b: A flower is built in rings, listed here from the outside inwards. The outer parts hold the flower together, protect it and, in many species, attract the animals that carry its pollen.
points: Receptacle: the swollen tip of the flower stalk, to which all the other flower parts are attached, so it holds the flower together. For example, in strawberry it swells to form the fleshy part of the fruit.

Sepal: a small, usually green, leaf-like part in the outer ring; together the sepals form the calyx. Sepals enclose and protect the flower while it is a bud, and some photosynthesise (make food using light).
Petal: inside the sepals; together the petals form the corolla. In insect-pollinated flowers the petals are large, coloured and often scented, which attracts insects.

Many insect-pollinated petals have lines or patches (nectar guides) that lead insects to the nectar. In wind-pollinated flowers petals are small, dull or absent, because there is no need to attract animals.

Nectary: a gland, usually at the base of the petals, that secretes nectar, a sugary liquid that rewards visiting insects so that they keep coming back. Pollen is also eaten by some insects, e.g. bees collect it to feed their larvae.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the function of named parts such as the sepal and petal. Sepal: protects the bud. Petal: attracts insects (large, coloured, scented in insect-pollinated flowers).

notes.b: The male part of the flower is the stamen. Its job is to make pollen, the package that carries the male gametes, and to hold it where a pollinator can pick it up.
points: Stamen: the male part, made of an anther on a stalk, the filament, so that the pollen is held up where it can be picked up. The stamens together form the androecium.

Anther: produces pollen grains by meiosis (a cell division that halves the chromosome number), so the pollen grains are haploid, with one set of chromosomes. Each pollen grain contains the male gamete nuclei. When ripe the anther splits open to release the pollen.

Filament: the stalk that holds the anther in position, where insects brush against it or out in the wind. It also carries water and nutrients to the anther through a small vascular strand (a thin tube of transport tissue).
Diagram: a stamen drawn on its own. Labels: anther, filament.
notes.tip: Stamen = anther + filament. A pollen grain is not itself the male gamete: it contains the male gamete nuclei.

notes.b: The female part of the flower is the carpel. It catches pollen, provides a route for the male gametes to reach the egg cell, and protects the ovules that become seeds.
points: Carpel: the female part, made of the stigma, style and ovary. A flower may have one carpel or many; the carpels together form the gynoecium.

Stigma: the tip of the carpel that receives (catches) pollen. It is sticky in insect-pollinated flowers, so pollen carried on an insect adheres, and large and feathery in wind-pollinated grasses, so it can catch pollen from the air.
Style: the stalk joining the stigma to the ovary. It holds the stigma in a position to receive pollen, and the pollen tube (the thin tube a pollen grain grows) grows down through it to the ovary.
Ovary: the swollen base of the carpel. It contains one or more ovules and protects them, so the developing seeds are not exposed. After fertilisation the ovary develops into the fruit.

Ovule: a structure inside the ovary that contains the egg cell (female gamete), made by meiosis, so it is haploid. After fertilisation the ovule develops into the seed. The micropyle is a tiny pore at one end of the ovule through which the pollen tube usually enters.
Diagram: a carpel drawn on its own. Labels: stigma, style, ovary.

Diagram: a half-flower (vertical section) of an insect-pollinated flower such as buttercup or wallflower. Labels: receptacle, sepal, petal, nectary, stamen (anther, filament), carpel (stigma, style, ovary), ovule.
notes.tip: Carpel = stigma + style + ovary. The ovule lies inside the ovary but is not one of the carpel's three named parts. Learn which part becomes what: ovary to fruit, ovule to seed.

notes.b: Pollination must happen before fertilisation can take place. Flowers can be self-pollinated or cross-pollinated, and several features favour cross-pollination.
points: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma of a flower of the same species. It is only the arrival of pollen: fertilisation, the fusion of gamete nuclei in the ovule, comes later.

Self-pollination: pollen is transferred to a stigma of the same flower or of another flower on the same plant. Cross-pollination: pollen is transferred to a stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species.

Cross-pollination combines genes from two different parents, so the offspring show more genetic variation. The species is better able to adapt to change, such as new diseases or climate, and avoids the harmful effects of inbreeding (breeding between close relatives).
Self-pollination needs no second plant or pollinator and is more certain, but it gives less variation. It suits isolated plants and plants in places with few pollinators.

Ways flowers favour cross-pollination: the stamens and stigmas of a flower ripen at different times; self-incompatibility, where pollen landing on a stigma of the same plant fails to grow a pollen tube; separate male and female flowers (hazel) or separate male and female plants (holly).

In primrose two flower forms exist: pin flowers, with a long style and low anthers, and thrum flowers, with a short style and high anthers. Insects carry pollen between the two forms, so the pollen reaches a different plant.

Agents of pollination (the carriers of pollen): insects (most showy flowers), wind (grasses and many trees, e.g. hazel, oak and birch), and less often other animals (birds and bats in other parts of the world) or water. There is more on this in Investigation: insect- and wind-pollinated plants.
notes.tip: Do not confuse pollination with fertilisation: pollination is the transfer of pollen; fertilisation is fusion of gamete nuclei. If asked to distinguish self- from cross-pollination, say whether the pollen lands on the same plant or a different plant of the same species. For an advantage of cross-pollination, say more genetic variation.

notes.h: The role of flowers in pollination
notes.b: The flower's structure matches the agent of pollination, whether an animal or the wind. Each type of flower is built to make the transfer of pollen as reliable as possible.
points: In insect-pollinated plants the flower attracts the pollinator (colour, scent, nectar guides), rewards it (nectar and pollen), and places its anthers and stigma where the insect's body touches them.
Pollen sticks to the insect at one flower and is rubbed onto the sticky stigma of the next flower of the same species it visits.
Many insects visit only one species on a foraging trip, having learned the flower they are faithful to, so pollen is carried to the right species.

Plant and pollinator both benefit, because the plant is pollinated and the insect is fed: this is a mutualism (a relationship in which both partners gain). There is more on this in Biotic factors and relationships.

In wind-pollinated plants the flower's job is to release very large amounts of pollen into moving air and to catch pollen on a large stigma. There is nothing to attract animals, so there are no showy petals, scent or nectar.

Sustainability link: many crops (e.g. apples, strawberries and oilseed rape) and wild plants depend on insect pollinators, especially bees. Bee numbers are falling through habitat loss, pesticides and disease.

Ireland's response is the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, first published in 2015 and coordinated by the National Biodiversity Data Centre. It encourages councils, farmers, schools and gardeners to provide food and nesting places for pollinators, e.g. by leaving wildflowers and mowing less often.
Health link: wind-pollinated plants, especially grasses, release huge numbers of small, light pollen grains that cause hay fever (allergic rhinitis) in early summer.
notes.tip: When relating a flower to its function, link each feature to its job: large coloured scented petals attract insects, a sticky stigma catches pollen from insects, and a large stigma catches pollen from the wind.

notes.h: From pollination to seed and fruit
notes.b: Once pollen reaches a stigma of the right species, a sequence of events leads to fertilisation. Afterwards the flower parts change into the seed and fruit.
points: Fertilisation in five steps: 1. A pollen grain of the same species lands on the stigma.
2. It grows a pollen tube down through the style to the ovary, digesting a path with enzymes.
3. The tube enters an ovule, usually through the micropyle, and carries the male gamete nuclei to it.
4. Fertilisation: a male gamete nucleus fuses with the egg cell nucleus to form a diploid zygote (a cell with two sets of chromosomes, the first cell of the new plant).
5. The zygote divides by mitosis (ordinary cell division that makes identical cells) to form the embryo.
Double fertilisation: a second male nucleus fuses with two other nuclei in the ovule (the polar nuclei) to form the endosperm nucleus, which divides to form the endosperm food store.

After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed, and its outer layers (integuments) become the testa, the seed coat. The ovary becomes the fruit, and its wall becomes the fruit wall (pericarp). The petals, stamens and usually the sepals wither and fall off.

Diagram: a carpel in section, with a pollen grain on the stigma, the pollen tube growing down the style and entering an ovule through the micropyle. Labels: pollen grain, pollen tube, style, ovary, ovule, egg cell, micropyle.
notes.tip: Exams ask which part becomes the fruit (the ovary) and which becomes the seed (the ovule); do not swap them. To outline events from pollination to the zygote, give the steps in order: pollen lands, pollen tube grows, nucleus fuses with egg cell.

keyTerms.definition: The swollen tip of the flower stalk to which all the other flower parts are attached.
A small, usually green, leaf-like part of the outer ring of a flower that protects the bud; the sepals together form the calyx.
A part inside the sepals that forms the corolla; large and coloured in insect-pollinated flowers and small or absent in wind-pollinated ones.
A gland, usually at the base of the petals, that secretes nectar to reward visiting insects.
The male part of a flower, made of an anther on a filament; the stamens together form the androecium.
The part of a stamen that produces pollen grains by meiosis and releases them when ripe.
The stalk that holds the anther in position and carries water and nutrients to it.
The female part of a flower, made of the stigma, style and ovary; the carpels together form the gynoecium.
The tip of the carpel that receives pollen.
The stalk joining the stigma to the ovary, through which the pollen tube grows.
The swollen base of the carpel, containing the ovules; it develops into the fruit after fertilisation.
A structure inside the ovary containing the egg cell; after fertilisation it develops into the seed.
A tiny pore at one end of the ovule through which the pollen tube usually enters.
The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma of a flower of the same species.
The transfer of pollen to a stigma of the same flower or of another flower on the same plant.
The transfer of pollen to a stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species.
A line or patch on a petal that leads an insect to the nectar.
A tube grown by a pollen grain down through the style to the ovary, carrying the male gamete nuclei to the ovule.
The diploid cell formed when a male gamete nucleus fuses with the egg cell nucleus.
The process in flowering plants in which a second male nucleus fuses with the polar nuclei to form the endosperm food store.

questions.prompt: Name the male and female parts of a flower and give one function of each of the anther, the stigma and the ovary.
questions.model: The male parts are the stamens, each made of an anther and a filament. The female parts are the carpels, each made of a stigma, a style and an ovary. The anther produces pollen grains by meiosis, and each pollen grain contains the male gamete nuclei. The stigma is the tip of the carpel that receives pollen; it is sticky in insect-pollinated flowers. The ovary is the swollen base of the carpel; it contains the ovules, protects them, and develops into the fruit after fertilisation.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between pollination and fertilisation in flowering plants, and give one advantage of cross-pollination.
questions.model: Pollination is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma of a flower of the same species, and it comes first. Fertilisation takes place inside the ovule: the pollen grain grows a pollen tube down the style to the ovary, the tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and releases the male gamete nuclei, and one male nucleus fuses with the egg cell nucleus to form a diploid zygote. One advantage of cross-pollination is that it combines genes from two different parents, so the offspring show more genetic variation and the species is better able to adapt to change, such as new diseases or climate. It also avoids the harmful effects of inbreeding.

questions.prompt: Draw a labelled diagram of a half-flower of an insect-pollinated plant and explain how the structure of the flower brings about pollination.
questions.model: The labelled diagram shows a vertical section of the half-flower with the receptacle, sepal, petal, nectary, stamen (anther and filament), carpel (stigma, style and ovary) and ovule. The large, coloured and often scented petals attract insects, and nectar guides lead them to the nectar at the base of the petals, which the nectary secretes as a reward. The insect's visit places the anthers where its body touches them, so pollen sticks to it. The sticky stigma is placed where the insect touches it, so pollen rubbed off the insect from a previous flower is caught. Many insects visit only one species on a foraging trip, so the pollen is carried to the right species, and the plant and pollinator both benefit.
